topic.subject: science
topic.title: Sound
topic.scope: vibration, medium needed, human voice and ear, amplitude, frequency, loudness and pitch, audible range, noise pollution

misconceptions.statement: Sound is a physical substance that flows through the air like a gas.
misconceptions.why: Students observe sound moving from a source to their ears and treat it as a material object.
misconceptions.fix: Sound is not matter; it is a form of energy that travels as a vibration through particles of a medium.

probe.question: If you pump all the air out of a jar containing a ringing bell, why does the sound stop?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the sound particles have no air to carry them out.

misconceptions.statement: If an object doesn't look like it is moving, it is not vibrating to produce sound.
misconceptions.why: Vibrations in many objects like a table or a bell are too small or fast for the human eye to see.
misconceptions.fix: All objects producing sound are vibrating, even if the movement is microscopic.

probe.question: Does a steel spoon vibrate when you tap it gently on a table?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it looks perfectly still.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Sound travels fastest in air because air is thin and offers less resistance.
misconceptions.why: In everyday life, we move through air more easily than through water or solids.
misconceptions.fix: Sound travels fastest in solids because the particles are packed closely together, allowing vibrations to pass quickly.

probe.question: Will sound travel faster through a wooden bench or through the air?
probe.wrong_answer: Through the air because wood is a solid block.

misconceptions.statement: Sound can travel through space because light from the sun reaches us.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the properties of light waves to sound waves.
misconceptions.fix: Unlike light, sound is a mechanical wave and requires a material medium to propagate; it cannot travel in a vacuum.

probe.question: Can two astronauts on the moon hear each other shout if they are not using radios?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sound travels through space just like sunlight.

misconceptions.statement: High-pitched sounds are always louder than low-pitched sounds.
misconceptions.why: Shrill sounds are often perceived as more 'piercing' or intense.
misconceptions.fix: Pitch depends on frequency, while loudness depends on amplitude; a high-pitched sound can be very soft.

probe.question: If a bird chirps very softly and a lion roars deeply, which has a higher pitch?
probe.wrong_answer: The lion, because its sound is much stronger.

misconceptions.root_belief: distinct properties of one thing are the same

misconceptions.statement: Loudness is determined by how fast an object vibrates.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the rate of vibration (frequency) with the force of vibration (amplitude).
misconceptions.fix: Loudness is determined by the amplitude of vibration, not the frequency.

probe.question: If you strike a drum harder, what changes to make it louder?

misconceptions.root_belief: more effort means more of every output

misconceptions.statement: The eardrum is a filter that chooses which sounds to let into the brain.
misconceptions.why: Students use biological 'gatekeeper' analogies for sensory organs.
misconceptions.fix: The eardrum is a thin membrane that vibrates in response to sound waves and passes those vibrations to the inner ear.

probe.question: What is the main job of the eardrum?
probe.wrong_answer: To decide which sounds are important enough to hear.

misconceptions.statement: Humans can hear any sound as long as it is loud enough.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the only limit to hearing is the volume of the sound.
misconceptions.fix: Humans can only hear sounds within the frequency range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, regardless of loudness.

probe.question: If a whistle produces a sound at 30,000 Hz very loudly, can a human hear it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if it is loud enough it will be audible.

misconceptions.root_belief: more of one input overcomes all limits

misconceptions.statement: Noise pollution only affects our ears and hearing ability.
misconceptions.why: Since sound is sensed by ears, students conclude the damage is localized there.
misconceptions.fix: Noise pollution can cause non-auditory issues like lack of sleep, hypertension, and anxiety.

probe.question: Can loud noise cause health problems other than deafness?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because sound only interacts with the ears.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single localized effect

misconceptions.statement: We produce sound using only our mouth and tongue.
misconceptions.why: The movement of the mouth and tongue is visible during speech, while the larynx is hidden.
misconceptions.fix: Sound is produced by the vibration of vocal cords in the larynx (voice box) in the throat.

probe.question: Where does the sound of your voice actually start?
probe.wrong_answer: In the mouth when the tongue moves.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Frequency is the total number of vibrations an object makes before it stops.
misconceptions.fix: Frequency is specifically the number of oscillations or vibrations per second.

probe.question: If a pendulum swings 10 times in 5 seconds, what is its frequency?

misconceptions.root_belief: a total quantity represents a rate

misconceptions.statement: Amplitude is the distance from the leftmost point to the rightmost point of a vibration.
misconceptions.why: Students measure the 'total width' of the movement instead of the displacement from the center.
misconceptions.fix: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a vibrating object from its central mean position.

probe.question: If a string moves 2cm up and 2cm down from its rest position, what is the amplitude?

misconceptions.root_belief: size is the total extent of an object
